## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)

Use RAII and smart pointers in tests:

TEST_CASE("Resource management", "[Memory]") {

    // Automatic cleanup on test completion/failure

---

`C:\b\minidbg\minidbg.exe <exe> [args]` (source `minidbg.cpp` beside it, built with `cl /std:c++17 /EHsc /DUNICODE`) runs a program under the Win32 debug API and prints a symbolized stack, with file:line where a PDB exists, for every access violation, heap corruption, stack-buffer overrun and second-chance exception. No WinDbg download needed. Set `_NO_DEBUG_HEAP=1`. `run-harness-example.ps1` there shows the env setup for the shell harness. Used 2026-10-14 to find the Check Print crash: the stack led straight to `GCodeViewer::init` → `strlen(glGetString(GL_VERSION))` with no current GL context.

For line numbers you need a tree with debug info. Configure with
`"-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE=/MD /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG /Z7"`, the same for C, and `"-DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS_RELEASE=/DEBUG:FULL /OPT:REF /OPT:ICF"` (example: `C:\b\ckp-build.cmd`). **Keep `/MD`.** Overriding the flags without it compiles everything `/MT`, and the link fails only at the very end with `LNK2038 RuntimeLibrary mismatch` against opencv/libcurl, after a 40-minute build. `SLIC3R_MSVC_PDB` is declared in CMakeLists.txt but nothing reads it.

Quick triage without any of this: the event-log fault offset in a system DLL maps to a function via `dumpbin /exports <dll>` (the nearest export at or below the offset). ucrtbase `0x2a341` is `strlen+0x31`, meaning a null or bad `char*`.

Run harnesses with `Start-Process -RedirectStandardError` rather than PowerShell `2>`. A PowerShell native-command redirect writes the file only when the process exits, so a hung run shows a 0-byte log. Visible windows of a stuck process can be listed with `C:\b\ckp-windows.ps1 -ProcessId <pid>` (a `#32770` titled 引导_P21 is OrcaSlicer's setup guide left open).

Windows GL fact found the same day: `wxGLCanvas::Create` on MSW always ends with `wglMakeCurrent(nullptr, nullptr)`. Creating any GL canvas leaves no context current, so GL work right after constructing a canvas needs an explicit make-current first. Upstream's helper for this is `GLCanvas3D::_set_shown_canvas_current`.

See [[windows-build-machine]].

10	
11	The JusPrin Windows verification box (Windows Server 2022, user `guitest`, as of 2026-09-09): no admin rights, no GPU, reached over RDP at 100% scaling. VS 2022 Build Tools, CMake and Ninja are installed; the deps live at `C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`. Main checkout `C:/src/JusPrin` is on `jusprin-newui` with a Release build in `C:/src/JusPrin/build`.
12	
13	**Why:** Several handoff items were blocked on machine facts (no debugger, no admin, DPI cannot change from inside an RDP session), so knowing them up front saves a diagnostic pass.
14	
15	**How to apply:**
16	- GL needs Mesa, and **every freshly configured CMake build tree starts without it** — nothing in CMake or the repo supplies it. Run `pwsh src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1 -BuildDir <build dir> -Source C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release` after configuring; it copies `libgallium_wgl.dll` and `dxil.dll` (from `C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Redist\D3D\x64\`) beside every GUI exe and `opengl32.dll` into its `mesa\` subfolder. Placement is not interchangeable, and each missing file has a silent signature — both documented in "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` (on `jusprin-newui` since 2026-09-13, commit `318208608f`).
17	- Quick recall of the signatures: no `libgallium_wgl.dll` → `glcontext not ready, postpone init`, no `got opengl version`, black canvas all session. No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. With all three present, both `d3d12` (default, `4.2 … D3D12`) and `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` (`4.6 … llvmpipe`) render.
18	- `slow_bootup` only moves the dxil crash from startup to first canvas paint; it is not a workaround.
19	- Lesson: a clear-only WGL smoke test passed under d3d12 because clearing compiles no shader, and was wrongly read as clearing the driver. A smoke test that skips the suspect code path proves nothing about it. (That test was removed from the repo for this reason.)
20	- A first-run datadir (e.g. copies of `C:\b\dd3`) logs ~630k lines in the first minute — the `GuideFrame::GetFilamentInfo` profile scan, driver-independent. Not a GL symptom.
21	- `D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` in the log is **Mesa's own d3d12 gallium driver on WARP**, not Microsoft's GLon12 mapping layer and not a real GPU. Confirm which GL is live by listing the process's loaded modules: the bundled Mesa shows `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (+ `DXIL.dll` once d3d12 has drawn), the unprovisioned fallback shows only `C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\OPENGL32.dll`.
22	- The permission guard has refused `Remove-Item` under `C:\b` in some sessions (reported as a protected path) and misparses `rd /s /q` and path-like string literals as delete targets. On 2026-10-23, in bypass-permissions mode with the user asking for the delete, `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force` under `C:\b` worked. Build trees there contain a `src\Release\resources` junction into a worktree: list links first (`Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Attributes ReparsePoint`) and remove each with `[IO.Directory]::Delete(<link>)`, which deletes the link only, before any recursive delete.
23	- A debugger can be had without admin: download `https://aka.ms/windbg/download` (an .appinstaller pointing at a ~1.2 GB msixbundle), unzip the bundle, unzip `windbg_win-x64.msix`, and `amd64/cdb.exe` runs directly. Set `_NO_DEBUG_HEAP=1` when running the harness under cdb, or teardown crawls in the debug heap for many minutes.
24	- Fixture directories for the harness's visual modes must be short paths (e.g. `C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\wp\...`); a long scratchpad path makes the profile-bundle copy exceed MAX_PATH and the fixture slice never validates.
25	- The harness prints everything on stderr; the exit code must be read with `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell (bash shows 127).
26	- DPI at 150%/200% needs the user to reconnect the RDP session at that scale. See [[jusprin-windows-parity-handoff]].
27	
28	Node is installed twice: the older `C:\tools\node` (v24.20.0), which is **not on PATH**, and
29	`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64` (v24.21.0, npm 11.19.0), added to the **user
30	PATH** on 2026-09-16. Check `Get-Command npm.cmd` before installing anything; a fresh Bash
31	session may still need `export PATH="$PATH:/c/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64"`.
32	
33	npm is not optional any more: since commit `5fc0efe2e3` the Agent and Home pages are built from
34	TypeScript and their `resources/jusprin/{agent,home}/index.html` is generated, not committed.
35	Without npm, CMake **fails at configure time** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Web/CMakeLists.txt`
36	`FATAL_ERROR`), so the first new source file you add breaks the build tree; and without the
37	bundles the app creates no Agent WebView at all, which shows up as `shell_agent_webview_created
38	FAIL` / "the Agent page did not complete its handshake" in the shell harness. Build them with
39	`npm ci && npm run build` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI` and `HomeUI`.
40	
41	The shell harness and the Agent page must come from the same commit: a harness exe built before
42	a page change hangs at `agent_reply_streams_to_completion` instead of failing.
43	
44	To work on `jusprin-mcp` (the MCP stdio helper) you do **not** need an app build, and a worktree
45	can have its own build tree in about three minutes: configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF`
46	(skips the npm requirement above) plus
47	`-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`, then
48	`cmake --build <dir> --config Release --target jusprin-mcp -- -m`, which compiles only the six
49	bridge/registry sources and `main.cpp`. `vswhere.exe` is **not** installed; vcvars is at
50	`C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\BuildTools\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvars64.bat`
51	and cmake at `C:\tools\cmake\bin\cmake.exe`. Point the Python suite at the result with
52	`JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE=<dir>\src\Release\jusprin-mcp.exe`; the whole suite runs in ~8 s.
53	
54	An **existing** build tree configured before node was installed keeps `JUSPRIN_NPM:FILEPATH=JUSPRIN_NPM-NOTFOUND`
55	in its CMakeCache, and `find_program` never retries a cached NOTFOUND -- so the next build fails at
56	configure with the `npm not found` FATAL_ERROR even once npm is on PATH. Reconfigure the tree once with
57	`cmake . -DJUSPRIN_NPM="C:/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64/npm.cmd"`; putting node on PATH alone
58	is not enough. Neither the Bash tool nor a PowerShell session started before 2026-09-16 inherits the user
59	PATH entry, so prefix `$env:PATH` explicitly in each invocation.
60	
61	**Shared build tree (2026-09-17):** other Claude sessions build and commit from `C:\src\JusPrin` and
62	`C:\src\JusPrin\build` concurrently. Do not patch that checkout or build there from a worktree session;
63	a link there holds `.lib` files and breaks their build (LNK1104). Use a separate tree instead: configure
64	with `-DBUILD_TESTS=ON -DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF -DSLIC3R_MSVC_PDB=OFF -DDEP_BUILD_DIR=C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build`
65	at a short path such as `C:\b\wsh`, which is a full `libslic3r_gui` build of about 40 minutes. To symbolize a crash
66	without a debugger, relink with a `ForceImportAfterCppTargets` props file (Link `GenerateDebugInformation`/`GenerateMapFile`),
67	read the fault offset from the event log (Application, event 1000), and run
68	`llvm-symbolizer --obj=<exe> --relative-address <offset>` (the symbolizer ships in the MSVC bin dir).
69	
70	- The in-app browser pane renders a `file://` page as a static snapshot and refuses `screenshot`.
71	  To look at a rendered page (e.g. a vitest `PREVIEW_OUT` page), serve the directory over a
72	  throwaway node http server on 127.0.0.1 and navigate to that instead.
73	
74	**Commits can hang in the `entire` hook (2026-09-25):** `git commit` from an agent session in a worktree
75	never returned; `entire hooks git prepare-commit-msg <file> message` alone hangs too (60 s, no output,
76	stdin closed). `--no-verify` does not skip prepare-commit-msg, and hooks must not be bypassed anyway, so
77	stop after one timed attempt (`timeout 90 git commit ... < /dev/null`), kill the orphaned `entire`
78	process it leaves behind (`ps -W | grep entire`), and ask Kenneth. Other sessions' commits carry an
79	`Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, so the hook works somewhere; the cause was not found.
80	
81	**Concurrent harness runs collide on WebView2 (2026-09-25):** every harness exe uses the same WebView2
82	profile, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\JusPrin2\EBWebView`. While another session's harness is running (e.g. a
83	long `--home-printers-live` fixture run), a second harness fails at once with
84	`shell_agent_page_handshake_complete FAIL`, and its app log shows `JusPrin agent page failed to load:
85	The group or resource is not in the correct state`. That is not a page or bundle problem. Check for
86	`shell_integration_harness.exe` in `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, don't kill another session's
87	process, and set `$env:WEBVIEW2_USER_DATA_FOLDER='C:\b\<tree>-webview'` for your own runs.
88	
89	**Scripting on this box (2026-10-06; Python corrected 2026-10-21):** no `python`/`py` on PATH, but Python 3.13 is at `C:\Users\guitest\.local\python-3.13.9\python.exe` and runs the prompt suites (`tests/project_prompt`, set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` and `JUSPRIN_TOOL_CALL_CHECK`). Otherwise use node (`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64`). Bash heredocs and `node -e "..."` that contain backticks, `${...}` or backslashes get mangled by the shell; write the script to a file with the Write tool and run `node <file>`. The main checkout's build tree `C:\src\JusPrin\build` (VS generator, Release) is fine to build from a session that is working in the main checkout: `cmake --build C:\src\JusPrin\build --config Release --target <targets> -- -m` after `vcvars64.bat`; harness exes there read `resources\` from the source tree, so `npm run build` in `AgentUI` is enough to refresh the Agent page. A touched `Workspace.hpp` rebuild of `libslic3r_gui` + `shell_integration_harness` takes roughly 10 minutes.

`icacls <dir> /deny "guitest:(OI)(CI)(W,D,DC)"` makes the folder **unreadable as well as unwritable**: icacls' "W" includes SYNCHRONIZE, and every normal file open (GENERIC_READ) asks for SYNCHRONIZE. Listing rights explicitly (WD,AD,WEA,WA) gets normalized back to W, so a read-only-but-unwritable folder can't be made this way. Verified 2026-10-23.

POSIX `std::filesystem::permissions` is ignored on Windows, which is why the shell harness's older `failed_autosave_*` checks fail there. The `--unavailable-storage` harness mode (commit fe6175df41, branch claude/autosave-unwritable) has an `UnavailableFolder` RAII helper: an ACL deny on Windows, chmod 000 elsewhere. Reuse it for any "storage went away" test.

Remove a deny with `icacls <dir> /remove:d guitest`. The owner keeps WRITE_DAC, so this works while the deny is in place.

Full Windows pass on 2026-11-01 at `b08a307459` (Release, `C:\src\JusPrin\build`). Scripts are in `C:\b\wk7`.

Fixed in the working tree on 2026-11-01, uncommitted when this was written (check `git log` before relying on it): the two test compile breaks, canvas overlays staying 1x above 100% (`canvas_ui_scale`), CRLF skill text, `snapshot(2.0)` drawing 1x, and the `--printer-setup` stall (`wait_for` now runs its own event loop; Preferences opened inside `wxYield` never got its web view started. Removing the yield fixed it; the inner reason is unproven).

Still failing on Windows:
- Default shell harness, 6 checks: `failed_autosave_is_visible`, `failed_autosave_has_plain_status_text`, `failed_autosave_blocks_project_release`, `earlier_model_version_available` (`std::filesystem::permissions` does nothing on Windows; the `UnavailableFolder` helper is the fix), and the 2 `agent_panel_columns_tile_*`.
- `--home-live` stalls at `home_live_page_shows_online`: Home v3 draws an idle printer as `.printer-chip`, and the harness reads the old card.
- ctest: PlaceholderParser coFloatsOrPercents segfault and `pick_attachment` previewText (CRLF in the test's own file). Workspace harness: `second_model_dropped`, `model_added_to_a_project_is_an_edit`.
- `tests/project_prompt/test_claude_cli.py`: `claude_cli.py` hard-codes `dir="/tmp"`.

**The shell harness exe ignores display scale on Windows:** it has no DPI-aware manifest, so it runs at 1x even on a 200% display, and a harness pass says nothing about scaling. Set `__COMPAT_LAYER=HIGHDPIAWARE` before starting it to get the real scale (`C:\b\wk7\s21.ps1`). `__COMPAT_LAYER=DPIUNAWARE` makes the DPI-aware real app run as if at 100%. With HIGHDPIAWARE, `cp_c_keyboard_selection_scrolls_into_view` fails because the panel is tall enough that its last row needs no scroll: a test assumption, not an app fault.

Real chat with no provider: `C:\b\wk7\mock.mjs` is a local Responses API stand-in. Start the app with `JUSPRIN_AGENT_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/responses` and a placeholder key in the scratch `JusPrin2.conf` (`conf-agent.mjs`: the file ends in an MD5 line, a hand edit without it is discarded). `chat.mjs` then drives the page with real typed input and wheel events over DevTools.

**Why:** Saves the next Windows pass from re-diagnosing these.
**How to apply:** Compare new failures against this list, and re-check anything here before quoting it, since fixes may have landed. See [[windows-build-machine]], [[native-ui-synthetic-input-and-capture]].

The RDP session can change display scale mid-run when Kenneth reconnects (100% to 200% on 2026-11-01). Whole-screen capture coordinates change with it, so re-read `query session` and the screen size if a click misses.

content.text:
Bug 1 and all three Windows test problems are fixed, and everything passes on this machine except a few failures in tests I didn't work on. Nothing is committed, and bugs 2 and 3 are untouched while the Mac check runs.

**Bug 1: print issues cut off above 100%**
- **Cause:** the print-issue boxes took their size from a value that stays at 1 on Windows, while the text grew with the display scale.
- **Fix:** they now use the real display scale. The tool strip, its value card and the Check Print caption had the same fault, so I fixed them too. The issue box also has to avoid the tool strip, so the two need the same scale.
- **Checked in the real app at 200%:** using the same file as before, the warning that read "Wh" now reads "Whole plate" in full. The before-and-after picture is sent.
- **Checked at 100%:** the test harness still draws the box at its original width.
- **Not changed:** list rows are still one line that stops at the edge, as they do at 100%. Pressing a row opens the whole message.

**Windows test problems**
- **CRLF skill text:** skills now reach the model with the same line endings from every build. A Windows build was sending different text, so this affected the product as well as the tests. All 623 Agent page tests pass.
- **2x pixel checks:** the test snapshot now really draws at double size, and all three checks pass.
- **`--printer-setup` stall:** the test's waiting method stopped Preferences from loading its page. With a different wait, all 252 checks pass. I don't know exactly why the old wait blocked it, only that removing it fixed the stall.
- **One extra failure:** that run reached a check no earlier run had, and it failed because its fake "can't save" folder doesn't work on Windows. I fixed that too.

**Full run on this machine**
- The whole project now builds, including the two test programs that didn't compile before.
- The other harness modes I ran pass, including the 12,934 prompt request checks.

**Still failing, none caused by this work**
- **Default harness mode:** 6 checks. Four are about failed autosaves, and two are about the agent panel columns.
- **Unit tests:** the same two as before, the PlaceholderParser crash and `pick_attachment`.
- **`--home-live`:** still stalls, as it did before.

**What to watch**
- **macOS and Linux not run:** the scale change should make no difference there, because wxWidgets' source gives the same number on both. The new wait affects every harness mode, though, so the Mac agent should rerun the harness.
- **The harness ignores display scale on Windows:** it normally runs at 100% even on a 200% display, so the new box-width checks only catch this bug with `__COMPAT_LAYER=HIGHDPIAWARE` set. In that mode one Check Print check fails, because it expects a list that needs scrolling, and at 200% it doesn't.
- **Possible new issue:** when I reopened the project, no print-issue pill appeared until I imported an object, even though the file has a blocking error. I haven't checked whether that's intended, or whether it happened before these changes.

Should I commit these fixes now along with the two compile fixes, or wait until the Mac agent has run them?

content:
Mac results for the two bugs. Both are code bugs and both reproduce on macOS. Nothing was changed on the Mac, and neither fix below has been built or tested.

Line numbers are from jusprin-newui at 69780c7af4. b08a307459 isn't on that branch; its equivalent is 1635438d4f. Print.cpp, Preset.cpp, Preset.hpp, PrinterOrigin.cpp and SetupCommands.cpp are unchanged between b08a307459 and 69780c7af4.

## Results on macOS
- Test A (new empty --datadir, no Bambu profiles, file passed as a command-line argument): both bugs match your Windows description.
- Test B (shell harness with --manual-mcp and --fake-printer): correct. The chip shows "from the file", Slice is active, and slicing finishes. I opened the file with the project_open tool, not File > Open, because the macOS file picker couldn't be controlled.
- Test B doesn't exercise the embedded preset. With Bambu installed, the file resolves to the system preset "Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle" (is_system true).

## Bug 2: missing "from the file" mark
Cause, confirmed in the debugger in Test A:
- Stored preset: is_project_embedded true, is_external true.
- Edited copy: is_project_embedded false, is_external true.
- load_external_preset sets is_project_embedded only on the stored preset (src/libslic3r/Preset.cpp:2711-2713). It sets only is_external on the edited copy (2721-2722).
- current_printer() (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/SetupCommands.cpp:102) reads the edited copy, so is_user() is true and it counts as a named printer.
- Forcing is_project_embedded to true in memory, along with the Bug 3 flag below, brought back the triangle and "from the file".

Suggested fix, untested: in current_printer(), get the origin from the selected preset, for both is_named_printer (line 106) and printer_from_file (line 119). Keep reading settings from the edited copy. This stays inside JusPrin's own code.
- Check that get_selected_preset() is usable there, since presets is a const pointer.
- Avoid changing Preset.cpp. That is upstream-owned code, and other is_user() callers may read the edited copy.
- tests/jusprin/test_printer_origin.cpp tests the function on its own, so it can't catch this. Add a test at the current_printer() level or in the shell harness, using a real 3MF load.

## Bug 3: Slice blocked
Cause, confirmed in the debugger in Test A:
- At the real Print::validate call, m_isBBLPrinter is 0, relative extruder addressing is on, before_layer_change_gcode is empty, and layer_change_gcode has no G92 E0. So the rule at src/libslic3r/Print.cpp:1733-1738 fires.
- PresetBundle::get_current_vendor_type (src/libslic3r/PresetBundle.cpp:612) only searches installed vendors for the printer model. It returned Unknown in Test A and Marlin_BBL in Test B.
- Forcing m_isBBLPrinter on at that rule, along with the Bug 2 flag above, enabled Slice and removed the Error. I did not slice in that state, so nothing shows the resulting G-code is good.

Upstream: the rule is in upstream/main (Print.cpp:2792-2797) and release/v2.4, from commit 61e2abfb2b9. The vendor lookup is identical to upstream/main. Blame on the Mac reaches these real commits rather than stopping at 56eb9a1a46. I compared source only and didn't run OrcaSlicer, so don't claim OrcaSlicer shows this bug.

Suggested fix, a hypothesis and not tested: when a 3MF's printer_model is in the bundled resources/profiles/BBL.json but the vendor isn't installed, install that vendor before the file's presets load, from JusPrin-owned code if there's a seam for it. The file should then take the same path as Test B, which already works on both platforms.

Don't do these:
- Don't widen get_current_vendor_type or is_bbl_vendor. They also drive the Bambu network agent and other UI gates. src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md says an embedded preset must not switch the agent.
- Don't just remove the rule or add an exemption to it. m_isBBLPrinter has 16 uses in libslic3r, including G-code generation, so the block would clear while the G-code is still produced as non-Bambu.

Stop and ask Kenneth if this can't be a small change, or if installing the vendor changes anything a person would notice. Compare these against Test A today:
- Test B showed "0.20mm Standard @BBL A1M" with 9 settings changed, where Test A showed "HSW_Kabelhalter(Tape_4_3MF.3mf)".
- Test B showed "Textured PEI Plate", where Test A showed "Smooth High Temp Plate". I didn't investigate why.
- Check that the Bambu printers don't start appearing as printers the person set up.

The two fixes are independent. Fix Bug 2 even if the vendor install makes it disappear for this file, because embedded presets from other vendors still take that path.

## Before and after
Follow AGENTS.md, including agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md before editing any OrcaSlicer-owned file.
1. Reproduce both bugs in Test A before changing anything.
2. After the fixes, Test A needs: triangle and "Bambu Lab A1 mini · 0.4 · from the file" on the chip; "From the file · not one of your printers" in the menu; Slice active; the G92 E0 Error gone; a slice that finishes.
3. Inspect the G-code against a Test B slice of the same file.
4. Rerun Test B and confirm it hasn't changed. Also open a non-Bambu file and confirm it isn't installing anything.
5. Ask for a macOS retest, because neither fix has run there.

1	# Fork stewardship
2	
3	**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.
6	
7	One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**
8	
9	- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
10	- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
11	- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.
12	
13	Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
14	
15	## The ten principles
16	
17	### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much
18	
19	**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.
20	
21	**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.
22	
23	**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?
24	
25	**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.
26	
27	### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
28	
29	**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.
30	
31	**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
32	
33	**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?
34	
35	**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.
36	
37	### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it
38	
39	**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.
40	
41	**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.
42	
43	**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?
44	
45	**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.
46	
47	### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism
48	
49	**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.
50	
51	**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.
52	
53	**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?
54	
55	**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.
56	
57	### 5. One seam beats many touch points
58	
59	**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.
60	
61	**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.
62	
63	**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?
64	
65	**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.
66	
67	### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict
68	
69	**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.
70	
71	**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.
72	
73	**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.
74	
75	**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.
76	
77	### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly
78	
79	**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.
80	
81	**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.
82	
83	**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?
84	
85	**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.
86	
87	### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went
88	
89	**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.
90	
91	**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.
92	
93	**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?
94	
95	**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.
96	
97	### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it
98	
99	**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.
100	
101	**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit
108	
109	**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.
112	
113	**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?
114	
115	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.
116	
117	## Before you finish
118	
119	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
120	
121	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
125	   ```
126	
127	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
128	
129	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
130	
131	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
132	
133	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
134	
135	## This fork's terrain
136	
137	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
138	
139	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
140	
141	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
142	
143	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
144	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
145	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
146	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
147	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
148	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
149	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
150	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
151	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
152	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
153	needed edits across eight upstream files.
154	
155	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
156	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
157	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
158	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
159	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
160	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
161	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
162	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
163	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
164	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
165	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
166	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
167	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
168	
169	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
170	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
171	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
172	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
173	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
174	page, silently.
175	
176	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
177	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
178	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
179	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
180	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
181	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
182	owned by Plater's event handler.
183	
184	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
needed edits across eight upstream files.

The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit
108	
109	**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.
112	
113	**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?
114	
115	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.
116	
117	## Before you finish
118	
119	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
120	
121	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
125	   ```
126	
127	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
128	
129	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
130	
131	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
132	
133	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
134	
135	## This fork's terrain
136	
137	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
138	
139	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
140	
141	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
142	
143	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
144	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
145	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
146	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
147	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
148	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
149	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
150	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
151	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
152	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
153	needed edits across eight upstream files.
154	
155	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
156	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
157	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
158	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
159	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
160	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
161	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
162	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
163	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
164	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
165	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
166	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
167	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
168	
169	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
170	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
171	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
172	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
173	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
174	page, silently.
175	
176	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
177	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
178	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
179	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
180	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
181	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
182	owned by Plater's event handler.
183	
184	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

$ink = [System.Drawing.Color]::FromArgb(25, 25, 30); $grey = [System.Drawing.Color]::FromArgb(80, 80, 90)
$title = New-Object System.Drawing.Font 'Segoe UI Semibold', 30
$body = New-Object System.Drawing.Font 'Segoe UI', 21
$tag = New-Object System.Drawing.Font 'Segoe UI Semibold', 21
$scale = 0.5
$panels = @(
  @{ F = 'C:\b\wk7\testA\bug2\menu.png'; T = 'NOW: Bug 2 fixed. Slice still grey, error still there'; Col = $blue; Y = 210; Crop = @(0, 60, 3456, 1540) },
  @{ F = 'C:\b\wk7\testA\sim\menu.png'; T = 'IF THE VENDOR IS INSTALLED: Slice active, no error, different plate and summary'; Col = $green; Y = 1060; Crop = @(0, 60, 3456, 1540) }
)
$bmp = New-Object System.Drawing.Bitmap 1810, 1910
$g = [System.Drawing.Graphics]::FromImage($bmp)
$g.Clear([System.Drawing.Color]::White); $g.SmoothingMode = 'AntiAlias'; $g.TextRenderingHint = 'AntiAliasGridFit'; $g.InterpolationMode = 'HighQualityBicubic'
$g.DrawString('Bug 3 needs a decision: what installing the Bambu vendor would change', $title, (New-Object System.Drawing.SolidBrush $ink), 40, 26)
$g.DrawString('The same 3MF on a brand-new data folder, in the real app on Windows. The lower picture has the vendor recorded as installed by hand; no Bug 3 code exists yet. Look at the Plate row, the Setup summary, the Slice button and the Notes card.', $body, (New-Object System.Drawing.SolidBrush $grey), (New-Object System.Drawing.RectangleF 40, 86, 1730, 110))
foreach ($p in $panels) {
    $img = [System.Drawing.Bitmap]::FromFile($p.F)
    $w = [int]$g.MeasureString($p.T, $tag).Width + 24
    $g.FillRectangle((New-Object System.Drawing.SolidBrush $p.Col), 40, $p.Y, $w, 38)
    $g.DrawString($p.T, $tag, [System.Drawing.Brushes]::White, 50, ($p.Y + 1))
    $c = $p.Crop
    $g.DrawImage($img, (New-Object System.Drawing.Rectangle 40, ($p.Y + 46), [int]($c[2] * $scale), [int]($c[3] * $scale)), (New-Object System.Drawing.Rectangle $c[0], $c[1], $c[2], $c[3]), 'Pixel')
    $img.Dispose()
}
$bmp.Save('C:\b\wk7\bugs-labelled\Bug-3-what-installing-the-vendor-changes.png'); $g.Dispose(); $bmp.Dispose()

Full Windows pass on 2026-11-01 at `b08a307459` (Release, `C:\src\JusPrin\build`). Scripts are in `C:\b\wk7`.

Fixed in the working tree on 2026-11-01, uncommitted when this was written (check `git log` before relying on it): the two test compile breaks, canvas overlays staying 1x above 100% (`canvas_ui_scale`), CRLF skill text, `snapshot(2.0)` drawing 1x, and the `--printer-setup` stall (`wait_for` now runs its own event loop; Preferences opened inside `wxYield` never got its web view started. Removing the yield fixed it; the inner reason is unproven).

Still failing on Windows:
- Default shell harness, 6 checks: `failed_autosave_is_visible`, `failed_autosave_has_plain_status_text`, `failed_autosave_blocks_project_release`, `earlier_model_version_available` (`std::filesystem::permissions` does nothing on Windows; the `UnavailableFolder` helper is the fix), and the 2 `agent_panel_columns_tile_*`.
- `--home-live` stalls at `home_live_page_shows_online`: Home v3 draws an idle printer as `.printer-chip`, and the harness reads the old card.
- ctest: PlaceholderParser coFloatsOrPercents segfault and `pick_attachment` previewText (CRLF in the test's own file). Workspace harness: `second_model_dropped`, `model_added_to_a_project_is_an_edit`.
- `tests/project_prompt/test_claude_cli.py`: `claude_cli.py` hard-codes `dir="/tmp"`.

**The shell harness exe ignores display scale on Windows:** it has no DPI-aware manifest, so it runs at 1x even on a 200% display, and a harness pass says nothing about scaling. Set `__COMPAT_LAYER=HIGHDPIAWARE` before starting it to get the real scale (`C:\b\wk7\s21.ps1`). `__COMPAT_LAYER=DPIUNAWARE` makes the DPI-aware real app run as if at 100%. With HIGHDPIAWARE, `cp_c_keyboard_selection_scrolls_into_view` fails because the panel is tall enough that its last row needs no scroll: a test assumption, not an app fault.

Real chat with no provider: `C:\b\wk7\mock.mjs` is a local Responses API stand-in. Start the app with `JUSPRIN_AGENT_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/responses` and a placeholder key in the scratch `JusPrin2.conf` (`conf-agent.mjs`: the file ends in an MD5 line, a hand edit without it is discarded). `chat.mjs` then drives the page with real typed input and wheel events over DevTools.

**Why:** Saves the next Windows pass from re-diagnosing these.
**How to apply:** Compare new failures against this list, and re-check anything here before quoting it, since fixes may have landed. See [[windows-build-machine]], [[native-ui-synthetic-input-and-capture]].

The RDP session can change display scale mid-run when Kenneth reconnects (100% to 200% on 2026-11-01). Whole-screen capture coordinates change with it, so re-read `query session` and the screen size if a click misses.

# CLAUDE.md

JusPrin — a long-lived fork of OrcaSlicer (open-source C++17 3D slicer, wxWidgets GUI, CMake build system).

## Upstream vs. fork attribution

This checkout holds two codebases: upstream OrcaSlicer (the `upstream` remote, SoftFever/OrcaSlicer) and the JusPrin fork's changes on top of it. Fork changes include everything under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the seams the fork added inside OrcaSlicer-owned files.

- Say "OrcaSlicer does X" only for behavior upstream ships. Behavior added by a fork commit is "JusPrin does X", even when it lives in an OrcaSlicer-owned file.
- Check before attributing; the file path is not enough. Run `git blame` on the line, then `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'`. No upstream branch containing the commit means the fork owns it. Run `git fetch upstream` first if the remote may be stale.
- If you have not checked, say it is unverified whether the behavior is upstream or fork.

## Error handling discipline

- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.

## Build Commands

```bash
# macOS
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Linux
cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo --target all --

# Windows (replace %build_type% with Debug/Release/RelWithDebInfo)
cmake --build . --config %build_type% --target ALL_BUILD -- -m
```

Node/npm is required to build the Agent and Home pages, or configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply the bundles.

### Building on a shared machine

Several agent sessions build on the same Mac at once. Without a limit, ninja runs one compile job per core plus two, so every build you start can take the whole machine. In 2026-10 one session stacked four builds in one build directory: 56 clang processes on 12 cores. It kept restarting its build to change targets and never limited the job count.

- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. If the load is already above the core count, wait or build less.
- Limit jobs: `cmake --build … -- -j4`.
- Decide the full target list before starting. Never restart a running build to add or change targets: let it finish, then build the rest.
- Run one build per build directory. Two ninja processes in one directory compete and can leave its records inconsistent.
- Stopping a build means stopping ninja. `pkill -f "cmake --build …"` kills only the cmake wrapper, and ninja keeps compiling. Start long builds in their own process group (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV' cmake --build …`) and stop them with `kill -- -<pgid>`. Then confirm with `pgrep -fl ninja` before building again.
- When a build is slow, count your own compile processes before blaming the load on other sessions.
- Reuse an existing build where the task allows. Ask before configuring a fresh full-app build the task does not require.

## Testing

Catch2 framework. Tests in `tests/` directory.

```bash
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure           # all tests
ctest --test-dir ./tests/libslic3r              # individual suite
ctest --test-dir ./tests/fff_print
```

Printer UI without hardware: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` (Bambu in-process fake). Isolated `--datadir`; do not drive another JusPrin instance.

## Code Style

- C++17, selective C++20. PascalCase classes, snake_case functions/variables
- `#pragma once` for headers. Smart pointers and RAII preferred
- Parallelization via TBB — be mindful of shared state
- Wording: a file or object is "opened", "imported", "loaded" or "added", never "arrived". "Arrive" is fine for messages, responses, events and lists. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards the text the model reads.

## Key Entry Points

- App startup: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp`
- Slicing pipeline: `src/libslic3r/Print.cpp`
- All print/printer/material settings: `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`
- GUI: `src/slic3r/GUI/`
- Core algorithms: `src/libslic3r/` (GCode/, Fill/, Support/, Geometry/, Format/, Arachne/)
- Printer profiles: `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`

## JusPrin Production UI

- Start with `agent-docs/jusprin/README.md` for the canonical product definition, production architecture, verification method, Orca integration guidance, and design system.
- Before editing any file outside `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, read `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`. Every line changed in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase, so those changes must be small, product-neutral, additive where possible, and accompanied by the rebase evidence that document requires.
- Experimental plans, probes, screenshots, logs, and temporary UI code remain on `jusprin-v2-poc`. Use `agent-docs/jusprin/poc-reference.md` for exact commit and path pointers; do not cherry-pick the POC wholesale.
- Curated brand and semantic UI assets live under `resources/jusprin/`.
- Before writing or changing any UI code, native or Agent page, follow "Writing UI code" in `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md`: every color, radius, font, and control size comes from the token file through `ShellTheme`, the shell recipes, or the CSS variables. A value with no token gets a token and a guard first, never a literal.
- Temporary working docs (handoffs, findings, plans written for another agent) stay untracked: never commit them, and never add them to `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude`. Untracked files in `git status` are how Kenneth tracks work that isn't finished.

## Critical Constraints

- **Backward compatibility required** for .3mf project files and printer profiles
- **Cross-platform** — all changes must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux
- Profile/format changes need version migration handling
- Dependencies built separately in `deps/build/`, then linked to main app

## Code review focus areas

- Changes must not cause regressions in existing functionality, defaults, profiles, or project compatibility.
- Features gated by options must not affect existing behavior when those options are disabled.
- Changes should follow the existing code style and architecture. Architectural changes should be justified in code comments and the PR description.
- Add helper functions or utilities only when existing code cannot reasonably be reused. Avoid duplication.
- Changes to OrcaSlicer-owned files must be additive where possible. Rewriting an upstream function, or reimplementing upstream behavior beside it, needs explicit justification in the PR description.
- When an upstream line is deleted or relocated, say where it went and what a future rebase must carry into the new home.
- Keep code concise and clear. Manually simplify AI generated bloated codes before review.
- Include targeted tests or documented verification for behavior changes, especially in slicing logic, profiles, formats, and GUI defaults.
